title: Legacy phosphorus mobilization by reactive silica amendments: from laboratory mechanisms to agronomic effectiveness in winter wheat
abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Historical manure applications on the Delmarva Peninsula created legacy soil phosphorus (P) accumulation, yet winter wheat ( Triticum aestivum  L.) often faces early-season P deficiency due to fixation in acidic soils. This study evaluated whether reactive silica (Si) amendments mobilize legacy P across three scales: laboratory chemical desorption, in-field pot plant uptake, and field trial yield. Methods A tiered approach used three legacy P soils. A 154-day incubation screened the desorption potential of silicic acid, Ca-Mg silicate slag, and switchgrass char. An in-field pot study isolated Si effects from liming effects using pH-balanced applications of silicic acid, silica gel, and slag. Finally, a field trial compared Ca-Mg silicate slag against standard lime and starter P practices. Results In the incubation, silicic acid and slag chemically mobilized P, while switchgrass char reduced water extractable P (WEP). In the pot study, reactive Si increased soil WEP by up to 70% and nearly doubled tissue Si, but did not enhance biomass or P uptake. Similarly, slag applied in-field did not alter soil P availability, though it significantly increased grain yield compared to standard management (8.25 vs. 7.58 Mg ha −1 ). Conclusion We hypothesize that pH-induced secondary Ca-P precipitation overrode Si-driven P mobilization. Furthermore, because yield improved without altering P nutrition, we hypothesize this field benefit was driven by Si-mediated stress resilience. Ultimately, while reactive silica chemically mobilizes legacy P, it cannot reliably replace starter P fertilizers. Heavy metal testing is recommended before applying slag in forage systems.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In regions characterized by intensive animal agriculture, such as the Delmarva Peninsula in the Mid-Atlantic United States, the long-term application of manure to agricultural land has fundamentally altered soil phosphorus (P) dynamics (Kleinman et al.  13 ; McDowell et al.  21 ). Historically, poultry litter was applied on Delmarva to meet crop nitrogen (N) requirements, resulting in P application rates that far exceed crop removal (Sharpley et al.  35 ). This imbalance has led to the accumulation of anthropogenic P (i.e., “legacy P”) in soils, with soil test P concentrations often exceeding the agronomic critical level (Shober et al.  35 ; Sims et al.  35 ). While soil P accumulation poses a significant risk for non-point source pollution and eutrophication of sensitive water bodies like the Chesapeake Bay (Kleinman et al.  13 ), a paradoxical challenge remains for producers: despite high soil test P, small grain crops such as winter wheat ( Triticum aestivum  L.) frequently exhibit early-season P deficiency (Grant et al.  8 ).

This agronomic inefficiency is largely driven by soil chemistry and climate. Winter wheat is planted in late autumn when soil temperatures are declining, which reduces the diffusion rate of phosphate ions (Grant et al.  8 ). Furthermore, many of these soils are naturally acidic Ultisols where P is strongly fixed by iron (Fe) and aluminum (Al) oxides (Sample et al.  33 ). To overcome these limitations, farmers typically apply inorganic starter P fertilizers (Grant et al.  8 ). While effective for yield, this practice further enriches the soil P pool, exacerbating the long-term environmental risk. Therefore, there is an urgent need for best management practices (BMPs) that can mobilize existing legacy P pools to meet early season crop P demand without additional P inputs.

The application of solid reactive silica (Si) amendments, such as amorphous silica and silicate slags, has emerged as a potential strategy to bridge this gap. Although not considered essential for all higher plants, Si is beneficial (if not essential), particularly for monocots like wheat, which accumulate Si in tissues to combat biotic and abiotic stress (Epstein  6 ; Tubaña and Heckman  35 ). When these solid materials dissolve in the soil solution as uncharged monosilicic acid (H 4 SiO 4 ) and approach Fe and Al oxides under acidic to near-neutral soil conditions, they form surface-reactive silicate species that compete directly with the orthophosphate anion for the same specific ligand-exchange sites (Koski-Vähälä et al.  16 ). However, because bulk solution H 4 SiO 4  remains uncharged at these pH levels (pKa = 9.7), it is a weaker competitor than the negatively charged phosphate anion. Therefore, a high, sustained concentration of reactive Si is required to overcome this thermodynamic disadvantage, shift the chemical equilibrium, and effectively drive P desorption (Koski-Vähälä et al.  16 ; Lee et al.  17 ).

However, the transition of this mechanism from the laboratory to the field has yielded inconsistent results. While some studies report enhanced P desorption and uptake following Si application (Lee et al.  17 ; Owino-Gerroh and Gascho  27 ), others report no effect or even reduced P uptake (Gao et al.  7 ; Ma and Takahashi  19 ). These discrepancies likely stem from the confounding effects of soil pH and the chemical composition of Si sources. The competitive desorption of P by reactive Si is highly dependent on ambient soil pH and the specific surface charge of Fe minerals in soils. Uhuegbue et al. ( 35 ) confirmed that Si physically displaces P on goethite and hematite surfaces, but this desorption weakens at higher pH levels as the positive surface charge of the Fe oxides decreases, altering the electrostatic binding environment. Furthermore, the introduction of Ca from slags may immobilize desorbed P as Ca-phosphate (Ca-P) precipitates (e.g., a “Ca penalty”), potentially masking the chemical benefits of Si. Common Si amendments, such as Ca silicate (CaSiO 3 ) minerals or slags and calcium-magnesium (Ca-Mg) silicate slags, act as liming agents. The resulting pH increase can mobilize P by reducing Al toxicity and often results in a rapid dissolution of Si; however, the rapid release of reactive Si is followed by an abrupt decline in porewater Si that can result in precipitation of Si rather than plant uptake (Teasley et al.  35 ). Moreover, the introduction of Ca with these sources can also immobilize P through the formation of Ca-P precipitates (Haynes  11 ; Sample et al.  33 ). Alternative Si amendments, such as amorphous silica gel or Si-rich plant residues (e.g., rice husk, straw) can serve as a non-liming source of reactive Si to soils; however, the availability of this Si to plants is governed by dissolution kinetics, which is affected by the source and its processing. For example, fresh Si-rich crop residues act as a slow-release, sustained source of Si that matches plant demand across the growing season. In contrast, combustion of these residues at high temperatures to form biochar can result in the formation of crystalline Si minerals (e.g., cristobalite), which effectively limits plant availability despite high total Si concentrations (Linam et al.  18 ; Teasley et al.  35 ).

Beyond its potential interactions with soil P, Si is known to enhance cereal crop yields by alleviating both biotic and abiotic stresses. In winter wheat specifically, Si deposition in the cuticle and epidermal cells provides structural rigidity that reduces lodging and susceptibility to fungal pathogens like powdery mildew ( Blumeria graminis ; Provance-Bowley et al.  31 ). Furthermore, Si fertilization has been shown to improve water-use efficiency and biomass production under deficit irrigation or drought stress conditions in grasses (Eneji et al.  5 ). Reactive Si amendments can also improve soil water retention, enhance aggregate stability, boost beneficial microbial abundance, and mitigate salinity and heavy metal toxicity (Schaller et al.  35 ). Industrial byproducts used as Si fertilizers, such as steel or blast furnace slags, also act as multi-nutrient amendments; unlike pure silicic acid, these materials supply significant quantities of Ca and Mg, while neutralizing soil acidity (Tozsin and Oztas  35 ). The agronomic value of these slags may therefore result from a synergistic effect of improved Si nutrition, pH correction, and the addition of secondary macronutrients.

This study employs a multi-scale approach, from laboratory to field, to disentangle the chemical potential of Si-driven P mobilization from the physiological and agronomic constraints that govern its efficacy in winter wheat production. We used three distinct legacy P impacted soils to evaluate Si efficacy across three phases: (1) a laboratory incubation to screen the chemical desorption potential of various Si sources (silicic acid, Ca-Mg silicate slag, and biomass char) without plant interference; (2) an in-field pot study designed to decouple the “Si effect” from the “liming effect” by maintaining stable conditions across treatments; and (3) an field trial to validate the agronomic viability of locally available Si amendments under realistic management conditions. We hypothesized that reactive Si sources would chemically displace sorbed P and increase water-extractable P (WEP) at the laboratory scale. Furthermore, we aimed to test if this chemical mobilization would successfully translate to the field scale, with the hypothesis that it would reduce agronomic reliance on starter P fertilizer for winter wheat.

sections.heading: Site description and soil selection
paragraphs: Soil samples were collected from three agricultural fields with a history of poultry litter application located in Sussex County, Delaware, USA. These soils represented major soils in the region: (1) a Fort Mott series (Loamy, siliceous, semiactive, mesic Arenic Hapludults); (2) an Ingleside series (Coarse-loamy, siliceous, semiactive, mesic Typic Hapludults); and (3) a Mullica-Berryland complex consisting of Mullica (Coarse-loamy, siliceous, semiactive, acid, mesic Typic Humaquepts) and Berryland (Sandy, siliceous, mesic Typic Alaquods) series.

Bulk soil was collected from the Ap horizon (0–15 cm) of each field using shovels. Approximately 0.21 m 3  of soil was excavated per site, air-dried, crushed to break clods, and passed through a 2-mm sieve. Soil samples were collected from the homogenized bulk soil prior to the incubation and pot experiments to establish baseline physical and chemical properties, and to determine lime requirements (Table  1 ). To accommodate the experimental timeline, bulk soils for the greenhouse pot study were collected first. Soils from these same three fields were collected approximately eight to nine months later for the laboratory incubation study. During this intervening period, the cooperating farmers applied agricultural lime to the fields as part of their standard management, which elevated the baseline soil pH of the incubation samples compared to the initial pot study samples.

The outdoor pot study was located at the University of Delaware Newark Farm in Newark, Delaware, USA (39° 40′ 5.91'' N, 75° 44′ 45.83 W). For the field validation trial, a separate site was established at the University of Delaware Carvel Research and Education Center in Georgetown, Delaware, USA (38° 38′ 7.13'' N, 75° 27′ 42.87 W). This site was selected due to favorable soil pH and because the fields where soils collected for the incubation and pot trials were not available for a large-scale field trial. The soil at the field site was mapped as a Pepperbox loamy sand (Loamy, mixed, semiactive, mesic Aquic Arenic Hapludults). While this soil possessed a slightly lower pH and Mehlich-3 P concentration than the pot study soils, it still met the necessary agronomic criteria for the study, representing a strongly acidic soil with “excessive” soil test P. Therefore, we recognize that study phases are related but are not directly comparable due to the lack of continuity in soil sampling timelines, management history (e.g. liming), and field locations.

sections.heading: Phase I: laboratory incubation
paragraphs: A 154-day laboratory incubation was conducted to evaluate the kinetics of P desorption by Si amendments. The study used a completely randomized design (CRD) with three replicates. Treatments included an unamended control, and three reactive Si sources applied at four “target” total Si rates (0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 Mg ha −1 ). The Si sources were: (1) Ca-Mg silicate slag (AgrowSil; Harsco Minerals, Sarver, PA); (2) switchgrass char generated from the combustion of locally grown switchgrass ( Panicum virgatum ) at the University of Maryland Wye Research and Education Center (Queenstown, Maryland, USA); and (3) laboratory grade, solid metasilicic acid hydrate (silicic acid; H 2 SiO 3 ; Sigma-Aldrich Co., St. Louis, MO, USA).

Prior to the initiation of the experiment, a subsample of the air-dried, sieved soil was analyzed to determine initial physical and chemical properties. Air-dried soil (230 g) was weighed into 240-mL polyethylene snap cups with holes drilled in the top to allow gas exchange; amendments were thoroughly mixed with the soil. Deionized water was added to bring the soil to 80% field capacity, as estimated in the lab using the method of Tan ( 35 ). Bulk density was estimated as part of the field capacity determination. Cups were snapped shut and incubated under ambient lab conditions (approximately 22 ℃). Soil moisture was maintained gravimetrically by weighing cups weekly and adding deionized water as needed.

Following routine moisture adjustment, approximately 12 cm 3  of soil was e collected from each cup at 0, 2, 7, 14, 28, 56, 90, and 154 days after treatment application to yield sufficient dry mass to complete soil extractions. Samples were air-dried and sieved (2 mm) prior to chemical analysis. Soil samples collected at all time points were analyzed for WEP and acetic acid extractable Si (AA-Si) to track release kinetics. In addition, samples collected at 56 and 154 were analyzed for pH, Mehlich-3 (M3) P, M3-Ca, and degree of P saturation based on M3 (DPS M3 ) to evaluate treatment effects on soil acidity and stable P pools.

sections.heading: Phase II: in-field pot study
paragraphs: A pot study was conducted to evaluate plant uptake and yield response under pH-controlled conditions at an outdoor pot-in-pot facility at the University of Delaware Newark Farm. Switchgrass char was excluded from this phase due to low reactivity observed in the laboratory incubation. The experiment used a randomized complete block design (RCBD) with three replicates. To isolate the Si effect from the liming effect, all treatments (except the Ca-Mg silicate slag) received reagent-grade CaCO 3  to raise soil pH to a target of 6.5 to match the predicted pH of the slag treatment.

The six treatments included: (1) a no Si control receiving only CaCO 3 ; (2) Ca-Mg silicate slag applied at a rate to meet the soil liming requirement, providing a target Si rate of approximately 0.41, 0.41, and 0.68 Mg ha −1  for the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils, respectively; (3) a “Low” silicic acid rate matched to the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (4) a “Medium” silicic acid rate at two times the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (5) a “High” silicic acid rate (2 Mg ha −1  target) with CaCO 3 ; and (6) silica gel (2 Mg ha −1  target; Sigma-Aldrich Co., St. Louis, MO, USA) with CaCO 3 . Calcium carbonate (lime) rates (adjusted for 100 Ca carbonate equivalence) were approximately 830 mg kg −1  for the Fort Mott and Ingleside soils and 1383 mg kg −1  for the Mullica-Berryland soil.

Plastic pots (12,452 cm 3 ) were filled with 16.5 kg of air-dried soil. Treatments (Si source and CaCO 3 ) were incorporated into the entire soil volume on 16 Nov 2015. Nitrogen, potassium (K) or manganese (Mn) fertilizers were also applied on 16 Nov 2015 based on University of Delaware recommendations for winter wheat to ensure non-limiting conditions (Shober et al.  35 ). Nitrogen was applied as ammonium sulfate to all soils at an N rate of 34.3 kg ha −1 . Potassium was applied as potassium chloride to Fort Mott and Ingleside soils at a K rate of 37.5 and 22.8 kg ha −1 , respectively. Manganese fertilizer was applied as manganese sulfate at a Mn rate of 22.8 kg ha −1  to the Mullica-Berryland soil only. Each pot was then thoroughly wetted and left fallow for a week to allow equilibrium of applied fertilizers and lime. Winter wheat was planted to achieve a seeding rate of 400 seeds m −2  (equal to 25 seeds per pot) in a greenhouse (to achieve rapid and uniform germination) on 24 Nov 2015. Once established (1 Dec 2015), pots were thinned to 12 plants per pot and moved to an outdoor, in-field pot-in-pot facility at the University of Delaware Newark research farm to simulate ambient field temperature and photoperiod conditions. The experimental pots were placed inside larger, in-ground pots (both equipped with drainage holes). The pots were allowed to drain and relied exclusively on natural precipitation for the duration of the 31-week outdoor growth phase, though soil moisture was not directly monitored. Climatic conditions (e.g., temperature and precipitation) were monitored by the Delaware Environmental Observing System ( https://www.deos.udel.edu/ ) weather station located at the Newark research farm (39° 40′ 10.2″ N, 75° 45′ 1.08″ W).

Ammonium sulfate was applied to all pots at an N rate of 66.9 and 34.3 kg ha −1  on 1 Apr 2016 and 2 May 2016, respectively to support late season growth. Plants were grown to physiological maturity (Feekes 11.4) and all aboveground biomass was harvested (24 Jun 2016). Harvested plant material was oven-dried at 65 °C and weighed. Wheat heads were hand-threshed to separate grain. Grain yield was weighed directly, and straw biomass was calculated as the difference between the total aboveground biomass and the grain weight. Grain and straw subsamples were ground to pass a 1-mm sieve prior to analysis for Si and P.

Initial operational soil P pools were characterized using a modified Hedley fractionation (Sui et al.  35 ) to determine the distribution of P between soluble (H 2 O-extractable), labile (NaHCO 3 -extractable), Fe/Al-bound (NaOH-extractable), and Ca-bound (HCl-extractable) fractions. Soil samples were collected to monitor nutrient dynamics throughout the growing season starting at 4 days after treatments were incorporated (20 Nov 2015). Subsequent sampling was conducted at 40, 80, 98, 129, 161, 189, and 239 days after amendments were applied using a 10-mL syringe to extract a composite core from each pot until harvest. All soil samples were analyzed for WEP, water extractable Si (WESi), and AA-Si to track P and Si release kinetics. Comprehensive chemical characterization (pH, M3-P, M3-Ca, and DPS M3 ) was performed on a subset of samples collected during early vegetative growth (Day 40) and post-harvest (Day 239).

sections.heading: Phase III: field validation trial
paragraphs: A field trial was conducted at the University of Delaware Carvel Research and Education Center to validate the efficacy of the Ca-Mg silicate slag under commercial field conditions. The experimental design was a RCBD with four replicates and plot dimensions of 4.6 × 9.1-m.

Treatments included an unamended control, a standard agricultural lime treatment (3.36 Mg ha −1  calcitic lime), an agricultural lime with starter P treatment (3.36 Mg ha −1  calcitic lime +25 kg ha −1  P), and a Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment applied at 3.36 Mg ha −1  to meet the liming requirement to achieve pH 6.5 (providing approximately 0.40 Mg ha −1  Si).

Phosphorus was applied as triple superphosphate at a P rate of 25 kg ha −1  (lime with starter P treatment only) and potassium sulfate was applied at a K rate of 102 kg ha −1  prior to planting to ensure non-limiting conditions. Lime and Ca-Mg silicate slag treatments were surface applied on 2 Nov 2016. All materials were incorporated via tillage. Winter wheat (SS8340, Southern States Cooperative, Richmond, Virginia, USA) was planted the following day using a grain drill at a seeding rate of 123 kg ha −1 . Urea ammonium sulfate was applied at an N rate of 36.4 kg ha −1  at planting (3 Nov 2016). Climatic conditions (e.g., temperature and precipitation) were monitored by the Delaware Environmental Observing System ( https://www.deos.udel.edu/ ) weather station located at the Carvel Center research farm (38° 38′ 9.96″ N, 75°27′18″ W).

Early biomass samples were collected at green up (6 Mar 2017), dried at 65 ℃, and biomass was recorded. Ammonium sulfate was applied at an N rate of 54.9 kg ha −1  and thifensulfuron-methyl (Harmony SG) was applied at 63 g product ha −1  on 6 Mar 2017. Grain was harvested at maturity (approximately 15 Jun 2017) using a small plot combine (Massey Ferguson 8XP; Kincaid Equipment Manufacturing, Haven, Kansas, USA); yields were adjusted to 13.5% moisture content. A grain subsample was collected from each plot, dried at 65 °C to constant weight, and analyzed for P and Si.

Soil samples (0–15 cm) were collected at four distinct agronomic stages: pre-plant (16 Oct 2016), dormancy (21 Dec 2016), green-up (6 Mar 2017), and post-harvest (19 Jul 2017). Samples from all four time points were analyzed for pH, WEP, M3-P, and M3-Ca.

sections.heading: Reactive silica amendment rates and characterization
paragraphs: Target (nominal) total Si rates were based on estimated Si contents of 120 g kg −1  for the Ca-Mg silicate slag (as provided by the manufacturer) and 343 and 467 g kg −1  for the silicic acid and silica gel based on theoretical stoichiometry; soil bulk density was assumed at 1.33 g cm −3 . The actual mass of the Ca-Mg silicate slag applied to the soils in the incubation and pot study was calculated using the elemental composition of the Ca-Mg silicate slag as determined via a semi-quantitative X-ray Fluorescence scan (XRF; Supermini200, Rigaku Americas, Inc., The Woodlands, TX, USA) performed by the Advance Materials Characterization Laboratory (AMCL) at the University of Delaware. The switchgrass char and a subsequent batch of slag were screened using a portable handheld XRF (S1 TITAN Handheld XRF Analyzer; Bruker Kennewick, WA, USA) strictly to provide a semi-quantitative estimate of bulk Si content to guide experimental application rates for the incubation and pot studies and the field trial, respectively. Reagent-grade amendments (silicic acid and silica gel) were characterized (post-hoc) for moisture content by drying at 105 °C. These values were used to calculate the “actual” elemental Si delivery for all experimental treatments. For ease of comparison, treatments are listed at the “target” rate in the manuscript.

sections.heading: Soil analysis
paragraphs: Initial soil characterization and experimental samples were analyzed using standard regional procedures. Particle size analysis was performed using the hydrometer method (Bouyoucos  2 ), and organic matter was determined by loss on ignition (Schulte and Hoskins  35 ). Soil pH was measured in a 1:1 (w:v) soil:water suspension; Adams-Evans buffer pH was also measured to estimate lime recommendations (Sims and Eckert  45 ). Soils were extracted with M3 solution (1:10 ratio of soil to 0.2 CH 3 COOH +0.025 NH 4 NO 3  + 0.015 NH 4 F + 0.13 HNO 3  + 0.001 M EDTA; 5-min reaction time; Wolf and Beegle  35 ), and concentrations of P, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Al in extracts were analyzed using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES; Thermo iCAP 7600, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA). The DPS M3  was calculated as the molar ratio of M3-P to the sum of M3-Al and M3-Fe, expressed as a percentage (Maguire and Sims  20 ).

Water extractable P and WESi (pot study only) were determined using a 1:10 soil:deionized water ratio shaken for 1 h, filtered (0.45-µm; Self-Davis et al.  35 ) and analyzed by spectrophotometer using the molybdate blue methods of Murphy and Riley ( 23 ) for P and Hallmark et al. ( 9 ) for Si. Acetic acid-extractable Si was determined using a 0.5 M acetic acid extraction (Korndörfer et al.  15 ), where 10 g of soil was shaken with 100 mL of acetic acid for 1 h, filtered, and analyzed by ICP-OES. Incubation soils receiving Ca-Mg silicate slag and silicic acid at target Si rate of 2 Mg ha −1  sampled at 154 d were also evaluated for CaCl 2 -extractable Si (0.01 M CaCl 2 ; 1 h shaking; Korndörfer et al.  14 ) because these treatments are known to inflate the AA-Si concentrations (Nonaka and Takahashi  25 ; Sauer et al.  34 ; Snyder  35 ; Wu et al.  35 ).

sections.heading: Plant tissue analysis
paragraphs: Wheat grain and straw samples (pot study only) were dried at 65 °C to constant weight and the mass was recorded; subsamples were ground to pass a 1-mm sieve. Sub-samples of straw and grain berries were analyzed separately for Si and P after microwave-assisted nitric acid digestion following the method described in Seyfferth et al. ( 35 ). Briefly, a 0.2 g subsample was digested using a modified nitric acid (HNO 3 ) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) method with digests analyzed via ICP-OES for P and Si. For straw samples, the nitric acid digestions resulted in the formation of an acid-insoluble Si gel pellet (phytoliths), which was dissolved in 2 M NaOH; solutions were analyzed for Si using a spectrophotometer with the molybdenum blue method (Hallmark et al.  9 ). Pellet formation was negligible for grain samples as determined by Si concentrations that were below the method detection limit following the NaOH step. As such, the NaOH step was deemed unnecessary and was omitted for grain samples.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: All statistical analyses were performed using SAS software (Version 9.4; SAS Institute, Cary, NC). Data were analyzed separately for each soil series and experimental phase to evaluate treatment effects under different soil conditions. The Kenward-Roger adjustment was applied to calculate denominator degrees of freedom to handle the unbalanced nature of including controls within the factorial design. Normality and homoscedasticity of residuals were verified for all models using the Residual Panel graphical diagnostics. Outliers identified via studentized residuals (> 3 × standard deviation) were removed prior to analysis, as the magnitude of these values suggested a likely experimental artifact, such as soil contamination during extraction, weighing errors, or incomplete filtration, rather than a true treatment effect (Table  S1 ). This resulted in removal of five data points from the incubation study and five data points from the outdoor pot study. Retaining extreme values violated the assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variance required for the ANOVA and regression analysis. Removing these extreme outliers stabilized the variance and ensured the validity of the statistical comparisons. Furthermore, exploratory analyses retaining these extreme values demonstrated that the artificial variance introduced by these extraction artifacts violated assumptions of normality and mathematically masked the significant temporal interactions observed in the true data. In addition, 13 straw samples from the plants grown in the Mullica-Berryland soils were inadvertently lost after nitric acid digestion; as such, these samples were omitted from statistical analysis due to the missing NaOH dissolution step. One whole plant samples from the Mullica-Berryland soil was lost due to rodent damage during storage.

Overall, the conclusions are supported by a large-scale dataset comprising 3,317 successful observations across soil and plant components, representing a 99.2% data retention rate. The high sampling density (specifically the 8-point temporal tracking of WEP and AA-Si) provides a high-resolution mechanistic view of Si-P dynamics. The minor omissions noted in the text (primarily physical straw sample loss for one soil series) do not affect the statistical power or the overall trends observed across the three diverse soil textures evaluated.

sections.heading: Mixed model analysis for soil chemical analysis, plant yields, and plant tissue analysis
paragraphs: Soil chemical properties were analyzed using a mixed model approach. For the incubation study, treatments consisted of a 3 × 4 factorial combination of Si sources and rates, plus an unamended control (13 total treatments). For the pot study, six treatments were evaluated, comprising five Si-amended groups (Ca-Mg silicate slag, silica gel, and three rates of silicic acid), and a non-Si amended control; the Si gel and silicic acid treatments also received CaCO 3  to match the lime rates of the Ca-Mg silicate slag. In all models, treatment, day (or date), and their interaction were considered fixed effects. To account for repeated measures on the same experimental units over time, a REPEATED statement was used with the subject defined as replicate(treatment). For the incubation study, AA-Si data were log-transformed to satisfy model assumptions.

The covariance structure varied as appropriate to address the correlation between sampling dates and ensure model stability. A first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] covariance structure was used for time-series variables (WEP, WESi, AA-Si) to provide mathematical convergence while accounting for temporal autocorrelation.

A mixed-model analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was executed for both the laboratory incubation and greenhouse pot study datasets; this analysis was restricted to dates when pH measurements were available. In this validation framework, WEP and M3-P served as dependent variables to explicitly isolate direct effects of reactive Si treatments from potential confounding variations in soil pH (i.e., ruling out secondary liming artifacts). Because certain Si treatments (e.g., Ca-Mg silicate slag) directly increase soil pH, we explicitly acknowledge that this ANCOVA estimates the Si treatment effect mathematically adjusted for pH but does not prove a physically ‘pure’ Si effect independent of these interconnected chemical changes. Reactive Si amendments (treatment) and day (or date) were treated as categorical fixed factors, while soil pH was integrated as a continuous, time-dependent covariate. Mirroring the primary models, individual experimental units (replicate cups or pots) were assigned as a random subject effect (random intercept/subject = rep) to account for nested repeated-measures covariance. Covariate significance and Type 3 fixed effects were evaluated across all locations with denominator degrees of freedom calculated via the Kenward-Roger method.

A standard mixed-model ANOVA with a compound symmetry (CS) covariance structure was used for remaining snapshot variables measured at limited intervals (pH, M3-Ca, DPS M3 ). When significant ( p  < 0.05) treatment × day interactions were observed for soil data, treatment effects were partitioned by day using the SLICE statement. Mean separations for both plant and soil data were performed using the Tukey–Kramer honestly significant difference (HSD) test. Letter groupings for mean separations at each sampling date (soil) or at harvest (plants) were generated using the PDMIX800 macro.

Planned orthogonal contrasts were used to further tease apart main effects within the unbalanced design. For the incubation study, we constructed contrasts to compare Si sources overall (silicic acid vs. alternative sources), control vs. Si amended (average of all Si-amended treatments against non-amended controls), specific Si source comparisons at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate, and individual Si sources rate response (0.25 vs. 2 Mg ha −1 ). For the pot study, planned orthogonal contrasts included comparisons of control vs. all Si-amended, the source effect (silicic acid vs. Ca-Mg silicate slag), and the rate effect (low vs. high).

Isotherm derived parameters (S max  and  k ) from the pot study, as well as wheat grain yield and tissue nutrient concentrations (P and Si; pot and field studies), were analyzed using a mixed-model ANOVA (PROC MIXED). Treatment was evaluated as a fixed effect, while replicate (block) was included as a random effect to account for the RCBD. For variables where the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation algorithm bounded the random block variance at zero, the block effect was removed from the covariance structure. Consequently, the model automatically defaulted to a CRD, pooling the block degrees of freedom into the residual error term to calculate treatment significance. Degrees of freedom were calculated using the Kenward-Roger adjustment. Mean separations were performed using the Tukey–Kramer adjustment (ɑ = 0.05) to maintain a conservative experiment-wise error rate.

sections.heading: Mixed-effects regression analysis
paragraphs: Continuous linear relationships between soil water-extractable phosphorus (WEP; dependent variable) and acetic acid-extractable silicon (AA-Si; independent continuous variable) were modeled using linear mixed-effects regression. The identical observations from the unamended control (0 Mg ha −1 ) were explicitly reused and incorporated into each individual amendment source group (silicic acid, Ca-Mg silicate slag, and switchgrass char). Reusing the same control observations served to anchor each independent regression at a shared zero-application threshold to establish a true experimental baseline. Models were executed via the MIXED procedure in SAS with a random intercept assigned to individual replicates (random intercept/subject = rep) to account for the non-independence of repeated temporal sampling within identical experimental units (replicate cups) over the 154-day incubation. Regression slopes (estimates), intercepts, and associated Type 3 fixed-effects significance thresholds were resolved independently by soil location and amendment source group. Denominator degrees of freedom were calculated using the Kenward-Roger method. All regression lines presented graphically are derived directly from these fixed-effects.

sections.heading: Initial soil properties and amendment characterization
paragraphs: Soils used in the incubation and pot studies were characterized as loamy sands (Table  1 ). The initial soils collected for the pot study had strongly acidic pH values ranging from 5.0–5.1. Soils collected from these same fields approximately eight months later for the incubation study had slightly acidic to near neutral pH (5.7–6.6); higher pH values for the incubation study reflected farmer management during the intervening sample collections. Additionally, the Pepperbox loamy sand utilized for the on-farm field trial had a strongly acidic pH of 4.8. All three soils exhibited “excessive” M3-P concentrations, ranging from 171–684 mg kg −1 , which is three to ten times the Delaware agronomic critical value of 50 mg kg −1  (Shober et al.  35 ). Consequently, the DPS M3  was high (27%–110%), exceeding the environmental threshold of 15% established for Delaware soils (Sims et al.  35 ). The Mullica-Berryland soil was distinct due to its higher organic matter content (42–55) compared to that of the Fort Mott (17–20) and Ingleside (20–21 g kg −1 ) soils, classifying it regionally as a “black soil” with higher buffering capacity. The Pepperbox loamy sand used in the field trial had a slightly lower, yet still excessive, M3-P concentration and a DPS M3  near the 15% environmental threshold (Table  1 ). Sequential fractionation analysis of initial pot study soils indicated similar total extractable-P concentrations among all three soils (134–188 mg kg −1 ) with more than 50% of P extracted by NaOH, followed by NaHCO 3 -P, HCl-P, and H 2 O-P (Table  S2 ).

Lime requirements for the pot and field studies were determined based on the initial pH and Adams-Evans buffer pH (Table  1 ). To isolate the effect of Si from the liming effect of the slag, calcitic lime rates were calculated to achieve a target pH of 6.5, matching the neutralization potential of the Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment (Shober et al.  35 ).

Semi-quantitative XRF analysis highlights distinct chemical profiles among the Ca-Mg silicate slag and switchgrass char amendments (Table  2 ). Both the Ca-Mg silicate slag and switchgrass char contained similar concentrations of Si. The Ca-Mg silicate slag was dominated by Ca and Mg, consistent with its utility as a liming agent, and contained appreciable Fe, Al, and Mn compared to other sources. The slag material also contained appreciable concentrations of trace elements including chromium (Cr), nickel (Ni), and molybdenum (Mo). In contrast, the switchgrass char contained lower concentrations of Ca and negligible Fe, Al, and trace elements compared to the slag. The switchgrass char did contain higher concentrations of macronutrients P, K, and S than the slag. The silicic acid and silica gel sources were purchased as high-purity synthetic amorphous silica with negligible metal cation content. Gravimetric analysis revealed that the water content was 50.5 and 51.5 g kg −1  for silicic acid and silica gel, respectively.

sections.heading: Water extractable phosphorus mobilization
paragraphs: A significant treatment × date interaction was reported for soil WEP across all three soils ( p  ≤ 0.005). Phosphorus desorption dynamics were strongly influenced by the solubility and chemical composition of the Si source, total Si rate, and soil chemistry. The application of switchgrass char consistently led to a significant reduction in soil WEP concentrations compared with unamended control across all these soils (Fig.  1 ; Table  S3 ). In the coarse-textured Fort Mott soil, WEP concentrations were highly dependent on both Si source and rate, silicic acid provided the greatest WEP mobilization at lower rates. However, the Ca-Mg silicate slag resulted in the highest soil WEP concentrations when applied at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate (7.98 mg kg −1 ) by the end of the incubation, significantly exceeding the silicic acid at the same rate ( p  < 0.0001). In contrast, the silicic acid significantly outperformed the Ca-Mg silicate slag in the Ingleside and Mullica-Berryland soils. In fact, the Ca-Mg silicate slag often resulted in a decrease in soil WEP compared to the control (as was seen with switchgrass char), especially when applied at the higher total Si rates. Fig. 1 Temporal kinetics of soil water-extractable phosphorus (WEP) mobilization in three legacy P impacted soils during a 154-day laboratory incubation. Panels represent ( a ) Fort Mott, ( b ) Ingleside, and ( c ) Mullica-Berryland soil series. Treatments shown here include Ca-Mg silicate slag, switchgrass char, and silicic acid at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate and the unamended control. Data points represent empirical raw treatment means. Error bars indicate standard error (SE) of the mean. A companion mixed-model analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) using soil pH as a continuous, time-dependent covariate indicates that variations in soil pH exerted no statistically significant main or interaction effects on water-extractable phosphorus (WEP) dynamics ( p  > 0.05 across all soils). Consequently, the observed legacy P mobilization patterns are verified to operate via direct Si-driven mechanisms independent of secondary liming artifacts, fully validating the presentation of unadjusted empirical values

Soil pH was integrated into the models as a continuous covariate (ANCOVA) for the core periods where pH was tracked (Days 56 and 154) to evaluate whether the effect of the reactive Si treatments on legacy P mobilization remained significant after adjustment for measured pH. Under this strict covariate adjustment, the pH term was not statistically significant for WEP or M3-P across any of the soils ( p  > 0.05), meaning minor fluctuations in soil pH did not drive P release. Conversely, the main effect of Si treatment remained highly significant. Consequently, the effect of the reactive Si treatments on legacy P mobilization remained significant after adjustment for measured pH.

When adjusted for pH, the treatment × date interaction was significant for soil M3-P was not significant across any of the soils ( p  > 0.05; Table  S4 ). However, the treatment main effect was significant for the Fort Mott and Ingleside soils ( p  = 0.0147 and 0.0161, respectively), whereas M3-P in the Mullica-Berryland soil was unresponsive to treatment ( p  = 0.0643). In the Fort Mott soil, overall M3-P concentrations in the unamended control remained significantly higher than in the Si-amended treatments ( p  = 0.0028). All soil M3-P concentrations remained solidly above the agronomic optimum (50 mg kg −1 ) throughout the study.

sections.heading: Soil WEP and soil extractable silicon relationships
paragraphs: A significant treatment × date interaction was observed for AA-Si across all three soil series ( p  < 0.001). Consequently, the effects of Si amendments are presented by sampling date (Fig.  2 ). Silicic acid application resulted in a rapid increase in AA-Si, which remained elevated throughout the 154-day incubation for all three soils. Application of silicic acid significantly increased AA-Si concentrations relative to the control across all three soils (Fig.  2 ). In the sandy Fort Mott and Ingleside soils, silicic acid (2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) maintained AA-Si levels between 12.8 and 17.2 mg kg −1  between Days 56 and 154. In contrast, Si release was more attenuated in the high-organic matter Mullica-Berryland soil, where AA-Si concentrations peaked at 11.7 mg kg −1  at the same application rate (Fig.  2 ). Fig. 2 Temporal kinetics of acetic acid-extractable silicon (AA-Si) release in three legacy P impacted soils (Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland) during a 154-day laboratory incubation. Treatments shown here include Ca-Mg silicate slag, switchgrass char, and silicic acid at the 2.0 Mg ha −1  target Si rate and the unamended control. Data represent means ( n  = 3) for each soil series. Error bars indicate standard error (SE) of the mean. The split y-axis scale was used in all panels to visualize the high reactive Si concentrations in soils amended with the slag treatment relative to other sources. The break in the y-axis represents the range from 35–140 mg kg. −1

Switchgrass char also increased AA-Si concentrations relative to the control, but soil-specific differences were evident. At the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate, switchgrass char application significantly increased AA-Si in all three soils. However, at the 1.0 Mg ha −1  Si rate, significant increases were observed only in the Fort Mott and Ingleside soils, whereas AA-Si levels in the Mullica-Berryland soil remained statistically similar to the control (data not shown).

Mixed-effects regression analysis confirmed a highly significant positive linear relationship between AA-Si and WEP in soils treated with pure silicic acid across all three soils (Fig.  3 a-c). The magnitude of this mobilization strengthened with increasing soil buffering capacity, with the steepest response observed in the Mullica-Berryland and Ingleside soils compared to the sandy Fort Mott soil. In contrast, the relationship between reactive Si and WEP in soils treated with Ca-Mg silicate slag was highly inconsistent (Fig.  3 d-f). The slag exhibited a significant positive relationship with WEP release only in the Fort Mott soil. However, the slag trended non-significantly in the Ingleside soil and presented a significant negative relationship in the Mullica-Berryland soil. Similarly, switchgrass char did not yield a positive trend with P release in any soil (Fig.  3 g-i), presenting non-significant relationships in the Fort Mott and Mullica-Berryland soils, and a highly significant negative relationship in the Ingleside soil. This reduction in WEP for the slag and char treatments coincided with significant increases in soil pH and M3-Ca (Table  S5 ). Fig. 3 Relationship between acetic acid-extractable (AA-Si) and water-extractable phosphorus (WEP) in soils treated with ( a - c ) silicic acid (H 4 SiO 4 ), ( d - f ) Ca-Mg silicate slag, or ( g - i ) switchgrass char during the laboratory incubation. Data points represent individual sample replicates across all sampling dates and application rates. Regression lines indicate a positive linear relationship in three legacy P impacted soil series ( p  < 0.001) amended with silicic acid ( a-c ), supporting the mechanism of competitive desorption of phosphate by silicic acid in acidic soils without pH-induced Ca interference

sections.heading: Impact of amendments on soil pH and mehlich 3-Ca
paragraphs: A significant treatment × date interaction was reported for soil pH with all three soils ( p  < 0.002; Table  S5 ). By Day 154, the application of the Ca-Mg silicate slag at Si rates > 1 Mg ha −1  rate resulted in significantly higher soil pH than for the control for all three soils; soil pH was 7.27, 7.4, and 5.73, respectively for Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate, 6.7, 6.8, and 5.4 for the 1 Mg ha −1  Si rate, and 5.97, 5.90, and 4.77 for the control. Application of the Ca-Mg silicate slag at the 0.5 Mg ha −1  Si rate also increased soil pH (6.33) compared to control (5.97) for the Fort Mott soil.

A significant treatment × date interaction was also reported for M3-Ca with all three soils ( p  < 0.03; Table  S5 ). By Day 154, the M3-Ca concentrations were statistically higher than the control for all three soils when the Ca-Mg silicate slag was applied at rates of 0.5 Mg ha −1  total Si or higher; application of the Ca-Mg slag at the 0.25 Mg ha −1  Si rate also resulted in higher M3-Ca relative to control for the Fort Mott and Mullica-Berryland soils. Application of the switchgrass char at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate also increased soil M3-Ca relative to the control in the Ingleside and Mullica-Berryland soils (933 and 800 vs. 767 and 633 mg kg −1 , respectively).

sections.heading: Soil phosphorus dynamics and sorption capacity (S max )
paragraphs: The treatment × date interaction was significant for soil WEP across all three soils ( p  < 0.007; Table  S6 ). The effect on P solubility was heavily dependent on Si source (Fig.  4 ). In general, the highest target rate of Si application (2 Mg ha −1 ) was required to increase soil WEP compared to the control. Application of silicic acid at the high target rate resulted in significantly higher soil WEP concentrations than the CaCO 3  control throughout the growing season in Fort Mott and Mullica soils (Fig.  4 ). In the Ingleside soil, silicic acid at the high Si rate increased WEP significantly at 4 and 40, but differences were not significant compared to the control at later dates. The Ca-Mg silicate slag resulted in an immediate spike in WEP (Day 4) in Fort Mott and Ingleside soils ( p  < 0.05), increasing WEP by approximately 30% compared to the control, but this effect was transient and did not persist through the growing season (Fig.  4 ). Silica gel had variable influence on soil WEP compared to the control, with similar response as silicic acid at the high (2 Mg ha −1 ) target rate in the Mullica-Berryland soil ( p  < 0.0001). In contrast, the effects of Si gel were better than the Ca-Mg silicate treatment, but less effective than the high rate silicic acid when applied to Ingleside soils; Si gel did not increase soil WEP in the Fort Mott soil. Fig. 4 Temporal kinetics of soil water-extractable phosphorus (WEP) mobilization in three legacy P impacted soils during a 239-day outdoor pot study. Panels represent ( a ) Fort Mott, ( b ) Ingleside, and ( c ) Mullica-Berryland soil series. Treatments included (1) a no Si control receiving only CaCO 3  to achieve pH 6.5; (2) Ca-Mg silicate slag applied at a rate to meet the soil liming requirement, providing Si at approximately 0.41, 0.41, and 0.68 Mg ha −1  for the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils, respectively; (3) a “Low” silicic acid rate matched to the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (4) a “Medium” silicic acid rate at two times the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (5) a “High” silicic acid rate (2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) with CaCO 3 ; and (6) silica gel (2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) with CaCO 3 . Data points represent empirical raw treatment means; error bars indicate standard error (SE) of the mean. To evaluate target amendment effects adjusted for treatment-induced variations in soil pH, a mixed-model ANCOVA was performed with soil pH integrated as a continuous covariate. The analysis indicates that the soil pH covariate did not result in a statistically significant effect (p > 0.05). Consequently, the effect of the reactive Si treatments remained significant after adjustment for measured pH

Because soil pH varied significantly among some treatments (Table  S7 ), it was necessary to confirm that WEP mobilization was driven by reactive Si rather than strictly by pH-induced changes in P solubility. When soil pH was included as a continuous covariate for Days 40 and 239, the positive effect of Si amendments on WEP remained statistically significant. For example, in the Fort Mott soil on Day 40, pH-adjusted WEP in the silicic acid and slag treatments (9.77–10.79 mg kg -1 ) remained significantly higher than the unamended control (7.88 mg kg −1 ; p  < 0.0001). This confirms that the observed legacy P mobilization is a direct result of the reactive Si amendments, independent of liming effects.

Unlike WEP, treatment × date interaction was not significant for M3-P or DPS M3  across all soils. In addition, these parameters were largely unresponsive to the Si treatments across the Ingleside and Mullica-Berryland soils. However, there was a slight but significant decrease in measured M3-P observed in the Fort Mott soil amended with silicic acid at the 2 Mg ha −1  target rate (Table  S7 ).

Analysis of P sorption isotherms at harvest revealed that Si amendments physically altered the soil’s capacity to bind P, but results were soil specific. In the Fort Mott soil, silicic acid (2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) significantly reduced the S max ​ to 51, compared to 72 mg kg −1  in the control ( p  < 0.0001; Table  3 ). A similar significant reduction in S max  was observed in the Ingleside soil (31 vs. 87 mg kg −1  in the control;  p  = 0.0034). However, in the high-organic matter Mullica-Berryland soil, no significant treatment effects on S max  were observed ( p  = 0.5719; Table  3 ), consistent with the lack of WEP response in the incubation phase.

sections.heading: Soil silicon solubility
paragraphs: Treatment effects on extractable Si varied by extraction method (Fig.  5 ). As reported for the soil incubation, AA-Si concentrations for the Ca-Mg silicate slag amended soils were inflated, consistently 2–3 times higher than AA-Si concentrations with silicic acid application (data not shown). The WESi treatment × date interaction was significant ( p  = 0.0046 and 0.015, respectively) for the Ingleside and Mullica-Berryland soils, but not significant for the Fort Mott soil ( p  = 0.053; Fig.  5 ). Overall, both the Ca-Mg silicate slag and the silicic acid significantly increased WESi relative to the control ( p  < 0.0001), but the magnitude depended on the source and rate (Fig.  5 ). The Ca-Mg silicate slag significantly increased WESi in all three soils ( p  < 0.0001), with increases ranging from 2.8–5.6 mg kg −1  over the control. While silicic acid provided a rapid, rate-dependent increase in WESi (with the highest rates achieving > 2 × the control levels), the Ca-Mg silicate slag was also an effective Si source, maintaining significantly elevated WESi levels comparable to the agronomic rates of silicic acid. Fig. 5 Temporal dynamics of available silicon fractions in the pot study. Panels ( a – c ) represent acetic acid-extractable silicon (AA-Si), while panels ( d–f ) represent water-extractable silicon (WESi) across the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soil series, respectively. Note the high AA-Si concentrations for slag treatments contrasted with their disproportionately low WESi concentrations. While the slag did increase WESi compared to control, the disparity between extractants indicates limited mineral dissolution compared to silicic acid sources. Treatments included (1) a no Si control receiving only CaCO 3  to achieve pH 6.5; (2) Ca-Mg silicate slag applied at a rate to meet the soil liming requirement, providing Si at approximately 0.41, 0.41, and 0.68 Mg ha −1  for the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils, respectively; (3) a “Low” silicic acid rate matched to the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (4) a “Medium” silicic acid rate at two times the Si loading of the slag with CaCO 3 ; (5) a “High” silicic acid rate (2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) with CaCO 3 ; and (6) silica gel (2 Mg ha. −1  target Si rate) with CaCO 3 . Data represent means ( n  = 3) for each soil. Error bars indicate standard error (SE) of the mean

sections.heading: Soil pH and Mehlich-3 Ca
paragraphs: Soil pH and M3-Ca concentrations responded to treatment application, with variations by soil type (Tables  S7  and  S8 ). Soil pH management efficacy varied by soil type and time. In the Fort Mott soil, pH values were statistically equivalent among treatments at Day 40 ( p  = 0.66), but significantly diverged by harvest (Day 239;  p  < 0.0001), with the slag treatment maintaining higher alkalinity than the CaCO 3  controls. In the Fort Mott soil, all Si-amended treatments resulted in soil pH values that exceeded the 6.5 target pH by the final harvest (Table  S8 ). The Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment resulted in a soil pH of 7.2, which was significantly above the CaCO 3  control (6.5). Conversely, in the Ingleside soil, while differences were evident at Day 40 ( p  < 0.001), soil pH converged by harvest, resulting in no significant treatment differences ( p  = 0.07). In the Mullica-Berryland soil, significant differences persisted at both sampling dates ( p  < 0.001), with the slag treatment consistently resulting in higher pH values than the CaCO 3  control.

The treatment × date interaction for M3-Ca was not significant for all three soils ( p  = 0.3277, 0.2191, and 0.6933, for the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils respectively; Table  S7 ), while the main effect of treatment was significant ( p  = 0.0108, 0.0028, and < 0.0001, respectively). In the Ingleside soil, application of the Ca-Mg silicate slag resulted in significantly higher M3-Ca concentrations averaged across sampling dates compared to the unamended control (which received high rates of CaCO 3  to balance pH). In both the Fort Mott and Mullica-Berryland soils, overall M3-Ca concentrations in the slag amended soils remained statistically equivalent to the control.

sections.heading: Crop yield and nutrient uptake
paragraphs:
Despite significant increases in soil P solubility (as evidenced by soil WEP) and reductions in sorption capacity (S max ) in silicic acid treatments, there were no significant differences in winter wheat grain yield between Si treatments and the CaCO 3  control across the three soil types ( p  > 0.05; Table  4 ). For straw biomass, no Si treatments significantly increased biomass relative to the control; however, application of the Ca-Mg silicate slag in the Fort Mott soil resulted in significantly lower straw biomass compared to the CaCO 3  control. Grain P concentrations were not significantly affected by Si treatment in any soil. While straw P concentrations remained largely unaffected across most treatments, the high-rate silicic acid treatment (2.0 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) did significantly increase straw P concentrations in the Fort Mott soil compared to the control (Table  4 ).
