Total P removal (grain + straw) did not differ between the CaCO 3  control and Si treatments ( p  > 0.05). However, plant Si uptake was highly responsive to treatment in the Fort Mott and Ingleside soils (statistical analysis of straw Si was omitted for the Mullica-Berryland soil due to sample loss). In the Fort Mott soil, wheat straw Si concentrations were significantly higher in all Si-amended treatments compared to the control. In the Ingleside soil, only the medium and high-rate silicic acid and the silica gel treatments significantly increased straw Si, whereas the Ca-Mg silicate slag and low-rate silicic acid treatments remained statistically equivalent to the control. Across both soils, the medium-rate silicic acid treatment (0.82 Mg ha −1  target Si rate) resulted in the highest overall straw Si concentrations. Furthermore, plants grown in pots receiving the Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment had straw Si concentrations that were three- to fivefold higher than the lime only control. While this magnitude of increase was statistically significant for plants grown in the Fort Mott soils, high intra-treatment variability resulted in a lack of statistical significance for plants grown in the Ingleside soils (Table  4 ).

sections.heading: Field soil and crop response
paragraphs: In the field trial on Pepperbox loamy sand, no treatment × date interaction ( p  = 0.5933) or main effect of reactive Si treatment on soil pH was observed (Table  S9 ). While soil pH increased significantly over time across all plots (date main effect  p  < 0.0001; Table  S9 ), all treatments remained statistically equivalent throughout the study.

Similarly, there was no significant treatment × date interaction or treatment main effect on soil P dynamics ( p  = 0.8433 and 0.9269, respectively). Mean soil WEP concentrations did not differ significantly between the Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment (4.34), standard calcitic lime (4.62), lime with starter P (5.27), or control (5.32 mg kg −1 ) treatments across the study. Similarly, treatments had no effect on M3-P ( p  = 0.7953) or DPS M3  ( p  = 0.9414) among treatments at any sampling date (Table  S9 ).

Mehlich-3 Ca concentrations showed a numerical increase in the slag-amended plots (reaching 733 mg kg −1  at harvest vs. 439 mg kg −1  in the control), but this did not result in a significant pairwise difference at harvest, and the overall treatment main effect was not significant ( p  = 0.3202; Table  S9 ).

Despite similar soil pH across all treatments and similar M3-P concentrations we noted a significant treatment effect on wheat yield ( p  = 0.0049), where the slag-amended soils had significantly higher yields (8.25 Mg ha −1 ) than all other treatments (mean = 7.35 Mg ha −1 ). No significant differences in early-season vegetative biomass ( p  = 0.6390) were observed among treatments (Table  S10 ). Furthermore, there were no significant treatment effects on grain P ( p  = 0.6237) or grain Si (p = 0.7691) concentrations.

sections.heading: Competitive desorption vs. precipitation as the mechanisms of P mobilization
paragraphs: While the contrasting outcomes across our three experimental scales may initially appear contradictory, they collectively serve as a scale-dependent filter that defines the practical limits of Si-driven P mobilization. Our laboratory incubation provided supporting evidence for the chemical potential of reactive silica to desorb legacy P from mineral surfaces in a controlled environment. However, our subsequent pot and field trials supports the hypothesis that soil buffering, Ca interference, and plant physiological constraints ultimately dictate its actual agronomic effectiveness.

Our results suggest that reactive Si amendments can mobilize legacy P in acidic agricultural soils, but the magnitude and direction of this effect are strictly governed by the chemical composition and dissolution of the amendment. The strong positive linear relationship between AA-extractable Si and WEP in incubation soils treated with pure silicic acid (Fig.  3 ) supports the “competitive exchange” hypothesis. In this mechanism, dissolved orthosilicic acid (H 4 SiO 4 ), which remains uncharged at moderately acidic to near-neutral pH, competes directly with negatively charged orthophosphate anions for specific ligand-exchange sorption sites on Fe and Al oxides (Koski-Vähälä et al.  16 ; Lee et al.  17 ; Schaller et al.  35 ; Uhuegbue et al.  35 ). Yet, the discrepancy between AA-Si and WESi results in the pot study explains why the Ca-Mg silicate slag failed to mobilize P. While AA-Si indicated a large pool of “available” Si in the slag treatment (approximately 44–54 mg kg −1  higher than control), the WESi data, which more accurately reflects the dissolved monosilicic acid in the soil solution equilibrium, showed only a minor increase (2.8–5.6 mg kg −1 ) over the control (Fig.  5 ). In contrast, the AA-Si concentrations in silicic acid-amended soils were only 3–4 times higher than the WESi concentrations. These results support the idea that the solid Ca-Mg slag amendment remained largely unreacted in the soil. Because uncharged H 4 SiO 4  is a weaker competition than the phosphate ion at these pH levels, a high and sustained elevation in dissolved H 4 SiO 4  is required to overcome this thermodynamic disadvantage and force desorption. Without a sustained supply of H 4 SiO 4 , competitive exchange with phosphate could not occur. This suggests that AA-Si overestimates the agronomically active dissolved Si pool in slag-amended soils, acting as a methodological artifact rather than a predictor of P mobilization (Wu et al.  35 ). Furthermore, even if minor Si dissolution occurred, the chemical composition of the slag actively worked against P mobilization. While reactive silica promotes P desorption, the simultaneous introduction of cations (e.g., Ca 2+  from slag amendments or background electrolytes) can counteract this effect. Increasing the ionic strength with background electrolytes has been shown to increase P retention and adsorption capacity, as cations like Ca 2+  promote secondary Ca-P precipitation and can displace native Al 3+  and Fe 3+  and form new P-binding complexes (Hamdi et al.  10 ). Therefore, the high Ca loading from the slag likely shifted the equilibrium toward the formation of Ca-P minerals, outweighing any minor desorption pressure from the silicate anion.

Critically, the P sorption isotherm data (S max ) from our pot study provides empirical support of this competitive sorption mechanism in a plant-soil system. The significant reduction in S max  observed in Fort Mott and Ingleside soils treated with silicic acid (Table  3 ) indicates that Si anions successfully occupied binding sites that would otherwise be available for P sorption. By physically blocking these sites, reactive Si shifted the equilibrium toward the solution phase. This aligns with findings by Schaller et al. ( 35 ), who observed that increasing Si availability mobilized P from Fe minerals in Arctic soils. Our results also corroborate the model of competitive adsorption described by Obihara and Russell ( 26 ) and Hiemstra et al. ( 12 ).

While the use of a 0.01 M CaCl 2  background matrix and the addition of CaCO 3  to balance liming potential caused the Si-amended Fort Mott soils to reach a higher pH (approximately 6.90) than the unamended control (6.50), the high-rate silicic acid significantly reduced S max  compared to the control. Higher pH levels and Ca loading thermodynamically favor the formation of secondary Ca-P precipitates, which can occur simultaneously with adsorption and theoretically increase P retention. However, despite this potential for secondary precipitation, the net reduction in S max  observed in this study is consistent with Si-driven competition for sorption sites being strong enough to overcome the opposing pressure of Ca-P precipitation in these soils.

However, the efficacy of the Ca-Mg silicate slag source was compromised by a “Ca penalty.” Unlike pure silicic acid, the slag lime alternative contained significant quantities of Ca and Mg in addition to Si (Table  2 ). Phosphorus solubility is highly dependent on the pH of the soil environment; in acidic soils, P availability is primarily controlled by strong adsorption to Fe and Al oxides, whereas at near-neutral and alkaline pH levels (typically > 6.5), inorganic P predominantly precipitates with Ca, forming sparingly soluble Ca-P minerals. The significant increase in M3-Ca observed in the incubation (Table  S4 ), coupled with the pH increase due to the liming action of the slag, supports the formation of stable Ca-P precipitates, thereby overriding the Fe and Al in the soils and the slag. In the Mullica-Berryland and Ingleside soils, where slag reduced WEP, the high Ca loading likely shifted the equilibrium toward the formation of Ca-P minerals or the formation of Ca-P-Fe ternary complexes that outweighed the desorption pressure of the silicate anion (Haynes  11 ; Penn et al.  29 ). Ma and Takahashi ( 19 ) similarly reported that while sodium silicate increased pH and Si, it did not always increase P availability in P-deficient soils due to complex soil chemical interactions. Our data suggests that in legacy P soils, the addition of Ca-rich silicate amendments may inadvertently stabilize soil P pools rather than mobilize them, effectively acting solely as a liming agent rather than a P-mobilizer.

sections.heading: Phosphorus sorption by charred biomass
paragraphs: The consistent reduction in WEP following switchgrass char application supports the hypothesis that thermal processing of biomass can negate the benefits of phytogenic Si. Despite adding total Si to the system, the char acted as a net P sink. This is likely due to the increased surface area and porosity generated during combustion, a phenomenon well-documented in biochar literature where surface functional groups and porous structures sorb phosphate (Chen et al.  3 ; Park et al.  28 ). Furthermore, we hypothesize that thermal processing fundamentally impacts Si speciation and, consequently, the sorption capacity of the resulting char. This hypothesis is supported by previous peer-reviewed work evaluating the effects of thermal processing on biogenic silica materials, which demonstrates that high-temperature combustion can form crystalline Si minerals that limit availability (Linam et al.  18 ; Teasley et al.  35 ). This finding is critical for defining BMPs; while returning crop residues to soil is a primary pathway for Si recycling (Puppe et al.  30 ; Vandevenne et al.  35 ), our results suggest that incorporating charred residues may exacerbate P fixation in the short term compared to the use of un-charred phytolith-rich residues that release Si more readily (Seyfferth et al.  35 ).

sections.heading: Methodological limitations in soil reactive silica and phosphorus testing
paragraphs: Our study highlights a significant methodological limitation in assessing plant-available Si in amended soils. The AA-Si overestimated Si availability in slag-amended soils by up to 24-fold compared to the CaCl 2  extraction in the incubation study; a result that was also noted by Wu et al. ( 35 ) for soils amended with Ca silicate materials. Similarly, the WESi concentrations for slag-amended soils in the pot study were typically tenfold lower than AA-Si concentrations in the same soils (Fig.  5 ). Acetic acid is aggressive enough to dissolve non-labile Ca silicates in the slag that are not available to plants under ambient soil pH conditions (Nonaka and Takahashi  25 ; Snyder  35 ). Conversely, the 0.01 M CaCl 2  extraction provided values that were consistent between source types and aligned with thermodynamic solubility limits. This supports the idea that for agronomic consulting, particularly where slag amendments are used, dilute salt extractions provide a more accurate index of the active monosilicic acid pool than acid-based extractants due to their analytical limitations (Miles et al.  22 ; Wu et al.  35 ).

A similar methodological limitation occurred when assessing soil P availability. As noted in our results, soil M3-P and DPS M3  were largely unresponsive to the Si treatments despite significant increases in WEP (Table  S6 ). This discrepancy between the significant increase in WEP and the lack of response in M3-P following silicic acid application is a known methodological limitation. Uhuegbue et al. ( 35 ) recently demonstrated that strong acidic extractants like M3 are unsuitable for measuring P availability in Si-amended soils, as the co-extraction of non-target Si decreases the efficacy of the M3 solution at extracting P. This artifact perfectly explains the slight but significant decrease in measured M3-P observed in the Si-amended Fort Mott pots at harvest. Therefore, water extraction provides a more accurate reflection of the shift of P into highly labile pools following reactive Si application.

sections.heading: Regulation of P uptake due to physiochemical disconnect
paragraphs: The transition from the laboratory to the pot study revealed a consistent decoupling of soil solution chemistry (WEP) from plant physiology (yield and P uptake). While WEP accurately measures the shift of legacy P into the most highly soluble and labile pool, it is an indicator of potential availability rather than a direct proxy for plant P uptake, as actual assimilation is modulated by plant physiological demand. Silicic acid applied at the 2 Mg ha −1  target Si rate increased WEP by up to 70% and reduced soil sorption capacity (S max ) in the pot study, yet this did not translate to increased biomass or total P uptake in winter wheat. This lack of agronomic response cannot be attributed to sufficient background Si in the unamended soils. Initial AA-Si concentrations for the Fort Mott, Ingleside, and Mullica-Berryland soils were highly depleted at 7.96, 4.17, and 6.18 mg kg −1 , respectively (Table  1 ). These baseline levels are substantially lower than established critical thresholds required to trigger a measurable crop response in winter wheat, which range from 80 mg kg −1  for biomass response (Xu et al.  35 ) to 93.5 mg L −1  (approximately 71.9 mg kg −1  for a mineral soil with a bulk density of 1.3 g cm −3 ) for grain yield response (Provance-Bowley et al.  31 ). Instead, we hypothesize that this lack of response is not a failure of the amendment, but a physiological regulation mechanism similar to that described by Ma and Takahashi ( 19 ).

Ma and Takahashi ( 19 ) observed that while Si promotes P uptake in low-P conditions, it can suppress excessive P uptake in high-P environments to prevent P toxicity and maintain favorable intracellular inorganic P levels. The soils in our study were agronomically “excessive” in P (M3-P > 100 mg kg −1 ), well above the agronomic critical level for winter wheat (Shober et al.  35 ). Therefore, we hypothesize that the wheat plants likely engaged homeostatic mechanisms to regulate P influx. Because baseline soil P was already sufficient to meet crop demand, the additional Si-mobilized P was rendered redundant for biomass production (Neu et al.  24 ; Schaller et al.  35 ). Consequently, because crop P removal is inherently capped by plant physiological demand, Si fertilization is not a reliable method for rapidly drawing down legacy soil P stores through enhanced plant uptake. Although the pot study was conducted outdoors under ambient weather conditions, the soil environment was highly optimized and thoroughly homogenized to specifically isolate the physiological interface of Si and P uptake. By controlling pH and incorporating uniform fertilizers, the experimental design minimized the specific abiotic and biotic stresses (e.g., drought, nutrient imbalances, or fungal pathogens) that Si is well-documented to alleviate (Eneji et al.  5 ; Provance-Bowley et al.  31 ). Therefore, we hypothesize that this relative absence of ambient environmental stress likely masked the potential yield-promoting benefits of applied Si. The resulting disconnect (where Si successfully increased WEP but failed to increase wheat yield or P uptake) defines a critical practical limit of the Si-P mechanism: because crop P removal is inherently capped by plant homeostasis, chemically mobilizing legacy P becomes biologically redundant in the absence of environmental stress. Furthermore, the thorough mixing of liming agents in the confined volume of the pots may have exacerbated chemical interactions between Ca and P, further limiting agronomic responses compared to a heterogeneous field environment.

sections.heading: Agronomic implications
paragraphs: The transition from mechanistic pot studies to field validation trials reveals that while Si-driven P mobilization is chemically valid, harnessing it for yield gain in legacy P soils is challenging. Rather than being contradictory, the contrasting outcomes between these scales serve as complementary demonstrations of agronomic reality. In the highly controlled pot study, intensive laboratory homogenization and reactive liming induced a severe “Ca penalty,” where rapid Ca-P precipitation neutralized localized P desorption. Consequently, although Si amendments nearly doubled straw Si concentrations, this accumulation did not translate into higher grain yield within the buffered, low-stress environment. Conversely, because the field trial was subjected to environmental heterogeneity and natural stressors, we hypothesize that the applied slag delivered Si effectively enough to provide stress resilience and plant health benefits, which ultimately drove the observed yield increase (Eneji et al.  5 ; Provance-Bowley et al.  31 ). Together, these scales demonstrate that while the application of Si to legacy P soils does not translate into a reliable tool for bulk P-mining, it remains a highly valuable agronomic strategy for preserving yield under environmental stress.

Consequently, Ca-Mg silicate slag should be viewed primarily as an effective liming agent and a source of plant-available Si for structural fortification (Epstein  6 ; Provance-Bowley et al.  31 ), rather than a reliable tool for “mining” legacy soil P. It is important to note that these field observations are restricted to the specific site and single growing season evaluated in this trial. The 2016–2017 season was characterized by a relatively favorable climate (i.e., a dry but warm fall, a mild winter that allowed for early dormancy break, and timely April and May rains), which resulted in robust overall grain yields ranging from 7.23–8.25 Mg ha −1 . Because of these specific environmental conditions, these results should not be broadly extrapolated. However, while regional agricultural reports noted that erratic spring weather caused minor yield drags in some fields, the observed yield increase in our Ca-Mg silicate slag treatment suggests the applied Si may have provided stress resilience against these fluctuations. Because initial soil Mehlich-3 Mg and Ca concentrations were at or near agronomic optimum (447 and 92.5 mg kg −1 , respectively), and the calcitic lime control did not significantly increase yield, the probability of an agronomic response to secondary Ca, Mg, or pH adjustment is small. Therefore, we hypothesize that the active Si in the slag preserved the crop’s yield potential against ambient spring stressors, though further multi-year trials are needed to isolate this effect.

In small grain production, restricted root growth and slow P diffusion in cold soils frequently induce early-season P deficiency, prompting producers to apply starter P fertilizers even on soils with “excessive” soil test P (Grant et al.  8 ). Because we only collected plant biomass at green-up and harvest, we cannot definitively quantify P uptake during the earliest vegetative stages. However, our field data clearly demonstrates that any potential early-season advantage provided by the direct addition of starter P (or by Si-mediated P mobilization) did not translate into a significant increase in final grain yield or total crop P removal (Table  S8 ). For producers, this implies that the application of starter P to legacy P soils is an unnecessary expense, and Si amendments should not be viewed as a requisite tool to replace it.

Furthermore, the physical scale and chemical reactivity of amendments dictate their efficacy. In the pot study, lab homogenization with highly reactive CaCO 3  created a “Ca penalty,” where sudden influxes of Ca likely neutralized localized P desorption through rapid Ca-P precipitation. Conversely, the coarse heterogeneity of the field trial allowed slag to neutralize soil acidity and deliver Si more effectively without widespread Ca-P precipitation.

Similarly, the increased P sorption following incorporation of switchgrass char supports the hypothesis that crop residues are unlikely to be a viable amendment for P solubilization. Finally, while silicic acid and silica gel showed the most promise for P mobilization in the lab, they remain cost-prohibitive for field-scale application. Moreover, evidence from our pot study supports the hypothesis that high concentrations of silicic acid may induce physiological responses in small grains that negate the benefits of increased soil P solubility. As such, there are currently no viable amendments available to growers that simultaneously maximize reactive Si and enhance legacy soil P availability. Future research should focus on intermediate Si sources, such as amorphous silica-rich crop residues (Seyfferth et al.  35 ), which may offer a middle ground between the high solubility of silicic acid and the heavy Ca-loading of industrial slags.

sections.heading: Environmental and safety considerations
paragraphs: Despite its agronomic efficacy as a value-added liming agent in grain production systems, the use of industrial byproducts like Ca-Mg silicate slag in production agriculture is not without potential environmental concern. Chemical characterizations of the Ca-Mg silicate slag used in this study (Table  2 ) and related mineral byproducts indicate highly variable concentrations of trace metals, including Cr, Ni, and Mo (Qin  32 ; Torlon  35 ). The liming effect of the slag can result in immobilization of cationic heavy metals, thereby reducing their phytoavailability and translocation to grain (Deus et al.  4 ), anionic elements such as Mo can become increasingly plant-available at higher soil pH. Given the measurable Mo content in the evaluated slag (≈107 mg kg⁻ 1 ), there is a distinct risk of Mo accumulation in plant tissues. As such, land managers should use caution when applying slag-based lime alternatives to forage or pasture crops where high Mo forage can induce molybdenosis (Cu deficiency) in grazing ruminants. Furthermore, while steel slag lime alternatives have historically been used in grain production systems where residues are removed or incorporated, environmental and food-chain risks remain. Therefore, we strongly recommend that comprehensive Cr and Mo analyses, alongside evaluations of leaching and soil-to-plant transfer, be conducted prior to the application of these amendments in either forage or grain production systems.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In conclusion, while reactive silica increased soluble P under some conditions, it did not consistently improve P uptake or yield. Biological homeostasis, environmental variability, and the “Ca penalty” of common agricultural amendments effectively neutralize P-desorption at the field scale. Therefore, reactive Si should not be promoted as a tool to mine legacy P or replace starter fertilizers.

Instead, the agronomic value of Ca-Mg silicate slag lies in its performance as a highly soluble, multi-nutrient liming agent that supplies plant-available Si to preserve yield under environmental stress. However, using these industrial byproducts requires rigorous batch testing due to variable trace metal content. Specifically, given the high Mo content of the evaluated slag, we strongly advise against its use in pastures or forage systems as a precaution against potential Mo-induced toxicity (molybdenosis) in ruminants. Future research on Si-driven P mobilization should pivot toward Ca-free, intermediate Si sources (e.g., silica-rich plant residues), and any further evaluation of industrial slags must include rigorous testing of heavy metal phytoavailability and forage quality. In addition, future work should include measurements of biotic and abiotic stress (e.g., disease pressure, lodging, etc.) to verify the hypothesized plant health benefits of reactive Si amendments.
